newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Clarke to show key pre-election budget.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke to show key pre-election budget.

text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday treads a delicate path between wooing voters and placating financial markets in a crucial pre-election budget overshadowed by an embarrassing leak.
Just hours before Clarke was to present his budget, a leading tabloid said it had been passed secret documents detailing tax changes.
But the Daily Mirror, saying it realised what chaos could be caused on international stock markets, decided to hand the papers back to Clarke's office.
The first edition of the paper, which supports the opposition Labour Party, made no mention of the furore.
A Treasury spokesman said news of the leaks would not affect the content of the budget, normally one of the most closely guarded secrets in British government circles.

Finance Minister Hugh Dalton resigned in 1947 after leaking details of tax rises to a journalist which appeared in print before he rose to speak in the House of Commons. Prime Minister Clement Attlee called Dalton "a perfect ass".
The budget is considered crucial to the outcome of Britain's general election which must be called by next May.

Clarke, fresh from rescuing the government in a spat with parliamentary supporters over plans for a single EU currency, must score another triumph if Prime Minister John Major's Conservative Party is to retain hopes of an election victory.
The Labour Party is currently 20 points ahead of the Conservatives in the opinion polls.

The budget Clarke will announce to parliament at 1530 GMT must avoid alarming stockbrokers and foreign exchange dealers. But Conservative members of parliament are desperate for tax cuts which could win voters back to them and save their seats in an election which must be held by May 22.
Major predicted two weeks ago that the budget would be "prudent and sensible".

He told MPs the government had battled hard and long for the low-inflation, steadily growing British economy which has been in evidence for the past year. "We are not going to throw away those hard-won advances," Major said.

A Reuters poll of 27 London economists found that they on average expect a 2.25 billion pound ($3.79 billion) tax giveaway from Clarke, enabling him to cut his forecast for 1996-7 government borrowing marginally to 26 billion pounds.

That might allow Clarke to cut the standard rate of income tax by a relatively modest penny to 23 pence in the pound, and to claim that the government is making a steady advance towards its proclaimed 20 pence target.
Clarke was forced to interrupt his preparations for the budget on Monday to defuse a furious internal Conservative row over the single currency.
"Eurosceptics" had voiced anger at what they saw as the government's attempt to smother debate over the rules for the currency which the EU hopes to introduce in 1999.
He said there was no possibility of these rules affecting Britain if it chose to remain outside a single currency.
This assurance, together with a government promise of an extended parliamentary debate on the issue ahead of a December 13 EU summit meeting, appeared to cool the internal party row. ($1=.5941 Pound)
